paragraphs.heading: The open water
paragraphs.text: The pelagic zone is the open, free water of the ocean, away from the shore. The word comes from the Ancient Greek pélagos, 'open sea'. You can picture it as an imaginary cylinder of water, a water column, running from the sea surface down to the bottom. Here sea life can swim freely in any direction, with no underwater landscape in the way.

paragraphs.heading: Size and neighbours
paragraphs.text: In all, the pelagic zone holds 1.33 billion km³ of water. Its mean depth is 3.68 km and its maximum depth is 11 km. It is set apart from two zones at the bottom of the sea. The benthic zone is the very bottom, including the surface of the sediment, and clams and crabs living there are called benthos. Just above it lies the demersal zone.

paragraphs.heading: What changes with depth
paragraphs.text: Conditions change as you go down the water column. Pressure rises, while temperature and light fall. Salinity, oxygen and micronutrients such as iron all change too. The column can be divided vertically into up to five layers, and how many there are depends on how deep the water is. Pelagic life becomes less as depth grows.

paragraphs.heading: The lit top zone
paragraphs.text: The zone at the surface is lit, and it is the only zone with enough light for photosynthesis. Nearly all of the ocean's primary production takes place here. About 90% of marine life is gathered in it, including plankton, floating seaweed, jellyfish, tuna, whales, sharks and dolphins. The pelagic ecosystem is based on phytoplankton. A boundary called the thermocline separates this warmer top zone from the much colder mesopelagic zone.

paragraphs.heading: The mesopelagic zone
paragraphs.text: The mesopelagic zone gets only a trace of sunlight, and its pressure is about 20 - 100 atm. Swordfish, squid, wolffish and some cuttlefish species live in it. Many of its organisms have evolved adaptations such as bioluminescence because sunlight is lacking. At night, some of its creatures go up to the epipelagic zone to feed. Heterotrophic bacteria are among its more abundant organisms, and they mainly feed on and break down matter falling from the zone above.

paragraphs.heading: Pitch black water
paragraphs.text: One zone takes its name from the Ancient Greek for 'deep'. It is pitch black, with no trace of sunlight apart from an occasional bioluminescent organism such as an anglerfish. Its temperature and salinity are stable. Most creatures there live on detritus called "marine snow" that falls from the zones above. Others, like the marine hatchetfish, prey on their neighbours in the zone.

paragraphs.heading: The deepest part
paragraphs.text: The deepest part of the ocean lies at more than 6,000 m, and its zone is named after the realm of Hades, the Greek underworld. Such depths are generally found in trenches. The deepest trenches reach 10,935 m at Challenger Deep, the deepest point on earth. Very few creatures live in this zone.
